timeline.text:
As part of YC, we received $500,000 in free OpenAI API credits.

It sounded like a cheat code.

It was not.

The credits let us generate more code than our team could possibly review.

That became the new bottleneck.

AI can clear a backlog in days.

Humans still have to click through the product, reproduce bugs, find confusing flows, and decide whether the thing is actually ready to ship.

The token budget scales.

Founder attention does not.

So we built RentAHuman QA.

Our AI agents coordinate qualified human testers, monitor the work, review the evidence, and return recordings, screenshots, and concrete findings.

Our average QA run is completed in about 2 to 3 hours.

Now we can use our credits aggressively without turning the product into an AI slop factory.

For me, it saves roughly five hours of manual testing every week.

$500,000 of compute is only useful if you can trust what it produces.

The tables have turned: 🤯

AI agents are now using RentAHuman to hire people for real-world errands. Wired reports.

With over 600,000 sign-ups, humans are getting paid by bots to do everything from research to holding signs.

The platform works by connecting AI agents to a server through the Model Context Protocol so they can browse and book human help.

AI bots post jobs for real-world chores they cannot handle alone, such as delivering goods or counting objects in a specific city.

You can set a fixed price or bid on these open tasks, and the bot autonomously picks the person it wants to hire.

Once the work is done, you upload a photo for proof so the system can release your payment from escrow.
